result.text:
Five of the biggest US banks now say that if you let a third-party AI agent into your account, whatever it does is on you. That includes the case where the agent gets hacked.

JPMorgan and Bank of America added this last month. This week Citi, PNC and Citizens followed. Citi's new clause also makes the customer responsible for anything hackers do with credentials an AI tool leaked.

There's one exception in Citi's terms: AI agents that Citi itself provides don't carry that extra liability.

Together these five banks hold about $9.6T in assets. So for most US users, a budgeting or bill-paying agent built by a startup now comes with a risk the bank won't cover.

If you're building finance agents, this changes the pitch. Read-only access through an aggregator API is much easier to sell than an agent that logs in with the user's password and moves money. And if your product does need to move money, users will ask who pays when something goes wrong. Have an answer before they ask.

He's done. It's over. As far as the selling goes, he's just a footnote. 

"Hedge funds and institutional money managers have been the most aggressive sellers of U.S. tech stocks over the past few months, while company insiders have shown a much more mixed picture—continuing scheduled sales in AI high-fliers even as some executives began buying dips.
According to prime brokerage and fund flow data from Goldman Sachs and Bank of America, the tech sell-off in late 2026 breaks down across each group as follows:

1. Hedge Funds (Heaviest Active Sellers)

Hedge funds led the retreat from technology and AI stocks throughout autumn 2026:
Fastest selling in a decade. According to Goldman Sachs Prime Book data, hedge funds dumped global and U.S. tech stocks in October and November 2026 at the fastest weekly pace in at least 10 years, pushing their net leverage down to a five-year low.
Semiconductors took the biggest hit. Hedge funds unwound long positions and added short bets across chipmakers and AI infrastructure names—going underweight on AI stocks for the first time since 2023—to lock in annual gains ahead of year-end and reduce exposure to regulatory and capital-spending uncertainty.

2. Traditional Money Managers (Largest Allocation Cuts)

Mutual funds, pension funds, and long-only institutional asset managers have also been steadily rotating out of tech:
Biggest cut since 2006. Bank of America’s November 2026 Global Fund Manager Survey revealed that institutional fund managers slashed their overweight allocations to technology stocks by the largest margin since June 2006.
Bearish hedging. Institutional desks have also been heavy buyers of downside protection—purchasing record amounts of put options on mega-cap chipmakers like Nvidia—driven by concerns that AI hyperscalers may scale back capital expenditures over the next six months.

3. Company Insiders (Heavy Early Selling, Mixed Recently)."
